He snuffed in every corner, in the barn, in the cow-shed, in the henhouses, in the vegetable garden, and found traces of Snowb al almost everywhere. He would put his snout to the ground, give several deep sniffs, ad exclaim in a terrible voice, "Snowbal \! He has been here\! I can smel him distinctly\!" and at the word "Snowbal " al the dogs let out blood-curdling growls and showed their side teeth. The animals were thoroughly frightened. It seemed to them as though Snowbal were some kind of invisible influence, pervading the air about them and menacing them with al kinds of dangers. In the evening Squealer cal ed them together, and with an alarmed expression on his face told them that he had some serious news to report. "Comrades\!" cried Squealer, making little nervous skips, "a most terrible thing has been discovered. Snowbal has sold himself to Frederick of Pinchfield Farm, who is even now plotting to attack us and take our farm away from us\! Snowbal is to act as his guide when the attack begins. But there is worse than that. We had thought that Snowbal 's rebel ion was caused simply by his vanity and ambition. But we were wrong, comrades. Do you know what the real reason was? Snowbal was in league with Jones from the very start\! He was Jones's secret agent al the time. It has al been proved by documents which he left behind him and which we have only just discovered. To my mind this explains a great deal, comrades. Did we not see for ourselves how he attemptedfortunately without success-to get us defeated and destroyed at the Battle of the Cowshed?" *Page 22* **Orwell, George : Animal Farm** The animals were stupefied. This was a wickedness far outdoing Snowbal 's destruction of the windmil . But it was some minutes before they could ful y take it in. They al remembered, or thought they remembered, how they had seen Snowbal charging ahead of them at the Battle of the Cowshed, how he had ral ied and encouraged them at every turn, and how he had not paused for an instant even when the pel ets from Jones's gun had wounded his back. At first it was a little difficult to see how this fitted in with his being on Jones's side. Even Boxer, who seldom asked questions, was puzzled. He lay down, tucked his fore hoofs beneath him, shut his eyes, and with a hard effort managed to formulate his thoughts. "I do not believe that," he said. "Snowbal fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed. I saw him myself. Did we not give him 'Animal Hero, first Class,' immediately afterwards?" "That was our mistake, comrade. For we know now-it is al written down in the secret documents that we have found-that in reality he was trying to lure us to our doom." "But he was wounded," said Boxer. "We al saw him running with blood." "That was part of the arrangement\!" cried Squealer. "Jones's shot only grazed him. I could show you this in his own writing, if you were able to read it. The plot was for Snowbal , at the critical moment, to give the signal for flight and leave the field to the enemy. And he very nearly succeeded-I wil even say, comrades, he would have succeeded if it had not been for our heroic Leader, Comrade Napoleon. Do you not remember how, just at the moment when Jones and his men had got inside the yard, Snowbal suddenly turned and fled, and many animals fol owed him? And do you not remember, too, that it was just at that moment, when panic was spreading and al seemed lost, that Comrade Napoleon sprang forward with a cry of 'Death to Humanity\!' and sank his teeth in Jones's leg? Surely you remember that, comrades?" exclaimed Squealer, frisking from side to side. Now when Squealer described the scene so graphical y, it seemed to the animals that they did remember it. At any rate, they remembered that at the critical moment of the battle Snowbal had turned to flee. But Boxer was stil a little uneasy. "I do not believe that Snowbal was a traitor at the beginning," he said final y. "What he has done since is different. But I believe that at the Battle of the Cowshed he was a good comrade." "Our Leader, Comrade Napoleon," announced Squealer, speaking very slowly and firmly, "has stated categorical y-categorical y, comrade-that Snowbal was Jones's agent from the very beginning-yes, and from long before the Rebel ion was ever thought of." "Ah, that is different\!" said Boxer. "If Comrade Napoleon says it, it must be right." "That is the true spirit, comrade\!" cried Squealer, but it was noticed he cast a very ugly look at Boxer with his little twinkling eyes. He turned to go, then paused and added impressively: "I warn every animal on this farm to keep his eyes very wide open. For we have reason to think that some of Snowbal 's secret agents are lurking among us at this moment\! " Four days later, in the late afternoon, Napoleon ordered al the animals to assemble in the yard. When they were al gathered together, Napoleon emerged from the farmhouse, wearing both his medals \(for he had recently awarded himself "Animal Hero, First Class," and "Animal Hero, Second Class"\), with his nine huge dogs frisking round him and uttering growls that sent shivers down al the animals' spines. They al cowered silently in their places, seeming to know in advance that some terrible thing was ab out to happen. *Page 23* **Orwell, George : Animal Farm** Napoleon stood sternly surveying his audience; then he uttered a high-pitched whimper.
